title: Stellar Glitter in a Field of Black
caption: The dwarf irregular galaxy KK 246, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
credit: ESA/Hubble & NASA, E. Shaya, L. Rizzi, B. Tully, et al.

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: KK 246 looks like glitter scattered over black velvet, quite unlike a spiral or elliptical galaxy. Also known as ESO 461-036, it is a dwarf irregular galaxy that sits inside the Local Void, a vast stretch of nearly empty space.

KK 246 is the only galaxy known for certain to live in this enormous volume, and 15 more have been tentatively identified there. The many other galaxies visible in the picture lie beyond the void and belong to other groups or clusters.

Cosmic voids are gaps in the web-like structure of the Universe where very few galaxies, or none at all, are found. The Local Void lies next to the Local Group and is at least 150 million light-years across. By comparison, the Milky Way is estimated to be 150 000 light-years across, which gives some idea of how empty this region is.
scale: The Local Void is at least 150 million light-years across, according to ESA/Hubble.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3 observed the galaxy in visible and near-infrared light, from 606 nm to 1.6 μm. The color assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The individual stars of this faint dwarf galaxy are far beyond what the eye can see, and part of the light is infrared.
